The Diamond�
At the April meeting of the Executive Council a brief
financial report was read by Brother Corcoran, Business Manager of the
Diamond, and a
general discussion followed of its program for the next year.
The Diamond, we believe, has been instrumental in reviving the real
Psi U spirit in many of our alumni who have not been closely in touch with
the Fraternity either through their own or any other chapter. It also has
encouraged and in a
large measure
helped form or revive Alumni Clubs and
associations that will materially aid our chapters as well as bind our alumni
closer together in their respective localities.
The chapters have actively supported the Board of Editors iu securing
subscriptions, and it is hoped that the subscriptions will gradually increase
to the number necessary to support the publication without chapter guar
antee.
The question of raising the subscri23tion price to two dollars and other
features of financing were discussed, but it was the unanim.ous opinion of the
Couneil that it would be best to "carry on" for the second year as we have
in the past year, and that by next Convention time radical changes would
be possible, after the Diamond was on a sound basis.
The financial report to the Convention will show a
slight working profit
on the first year, made possible by each chapter paying its fee of a hundred
dollars. It will be impossible for the Business Manager of the Diamond

12
to file a complete financial report for the .first fiscal year until after the
June number is issued�
and we ask that the Convention grant him per
mission to file it then, to be incorporated in the minutes of the Convention,
upon the approval of the Executive Couneil. Brother Corcoran has recom
mended tnat two chapter.s�
the Iota and the Beta Beta�
be granted per
mission to have their guarantee reduced to fifty dollars for the next year,
as these chapters are numerically smaller than the others, and in this way
may be permitted to assume a more equal proportionate share.
"
Annual Taxes: Since 1917 until the present year no annual taxes have
been imisosed upon or collected from the chapters. These taxes include the
seventy-five cents required by the constitution for the Convention Fund and
the $2.25 provided by General Resolution No. 3 of 1906 for the general fund, �
totaling three dollars to be paid by each chapter for every active member
on its rolls on February 1 each year. This tax of three dollars per capita
is believed to be less than the average tax among other fraternities. The
Council, after considering its expenses, and the obvious fairness of reim
bursing Council members for actual cost of travel, of visits to chapters and
attending meetings, has voted to recommend that this Convention increase
the annual dues to five dollars for active members. This may be done by a
resolution raising the general fund contribution as now
provided by General
Resolution No. 3 of 1906 so as to make the amount thereof $4.25 as a tax
due from each chapter for every active member on its rolls on February 1
of each j'ear.
Chapter Bookkeeping: Various inquiries have been addressed to the
Council as to the best method of keeping accurate and practical accounts
of all chapter receipts and disbursements. Several of the chapters have
already adopted methods and we suggest that if time permits the delegates
of these chapters announce to the Convention the systems that have proved
satisfactory.
Liquor in Chapter Houses: Apart from legislation, whether state or.
national, upon the subject of intoxicating beverages, we should esteem it the
part of wisdom for every chapter to adopt and enforce a rule forbidding the
use of liquor within the chapter house, or upon the chapter property, and if
possible to encourage total abstinence during the formative period of under
graduate life.
EJxpuLsiON of Members : With deep regret we have to report the expul
sion from the Fraternity of Albert Spencer Danes, Iota '21, November 1920,
and Seymour Whiting Ely, Xi '24, February 1921, for gross dishonesty.

REPORT OF THE TREASURER
Following the receipt by the 1921 convention of a
temporary report by
the treasurer, a resolution ^^'as passed granting, leave to submit and substi
tute this permanent report in these printed proceedings of the convention.
During the past year the council approved the treasurer's suggestion
that fire insurance be placed upon our archives in the Brooklyn Warehouse
& Storage Company's care. A binder has been placed on this risk and policy
will be written when a proper inventory is made.
The Metropolitan Trust Company of New York is the custodian of the
investment securities, which consist of one industrial and eight railroad
bonds, on whieh the interest is promptly paid. The trust company collects
such income, and credits it to the council's bank account of which it is also
the dejiositary. For such custody, and services we pay the trust company
five per cent, on the coupons collected.

AUDITORS' CERTIFICATE
We have examined the books and accounts of
The Executive Council of the Psi Upsilon Fraternity
for the period from August 15th, 1918 to May 15th, 1921, and we hereby
CERTIFY that in our opinion the accompanying Balance Sheet as at May
15th, 1921, and Income and Expenditure Accounts, exhibit a correct view
of the financial affairs of the Council as shown by the books, subject to the
remark that the valuation of the Investments at cost is in excess of the
market value at May 15th, 1921.
All disbursements have been sufficiently vouched.
The securities representing the investments are in safe keeping with the
Metropolitan Trust Company according to their certificate of May 16th,
1921, and the balance in bank has been verified by certificate received from
the Bankers.
(Signed) Lingley, Baird & Dixon,
Accountants and Auditors.
